## The pipeline

```
tracker.api / create → tracker.scaffold → client drops into Shared/ → tracker.filer → tracker.scanner → tracker.reminder (on DRAFT_WEEKDAY) → tracker.view (the last step of every pass) → a person sends the draft
```

DECISION 107 - THE CACHE LEFT THE SYNCED FOLDER: ContentCache(engagement_dir) loads the engagement's memos and verdicts from the store's two tables (store.cached_verdicts()) once, works in memory as it always did, and save() writes what it learned and forgot through store.remember_verdicts() - one immediate transaction of the store's own, under the engagement lock, never store.record(), because a verdict is a derivation of the bytes and the rules and not an event; a pass killed mid-save leaves the previous rows. ContentCache() with no engagement is memory only (the CLI's, a test's) and its save() touches nothing. The engagement must already be in the store or the constructor refuses by name. The JSON cache file that used to sit in the engagement folder is never read; RETIRED_CACHE_FILENAME survives only for the filer's tidy-up, which removes it. THE STEP-0 RE-RUN'S FINDING: decision 105 had kept a two-form split's second verdict in the cache alone, so a rebuilt store read the second copy the ordinary way and failed it - the cache was carrying a decision, not a derivation. own_forms(text) is now the one reading of which forms a page counts as its own (the set of self-named forms when MULTI_FORM_FAMILIES or more families print their own name, else None; the constant moved here from the router, which re-exports it for one release); _check_uncached() reads through it, so the scan's miss verdict is the router's kept verdict for every page, split included, and a delete-and-rebuild leaves every status byte-identical. _evidence_from_json() takes a tuple as well as a list, so a verdict read back in the pass that kept it carries its evidence. Decision 55: contains_keyword() treats a hyphen-joined form variant as part of the form's name (1098 never matches 1098-T); a verdict that is the machine's (no OCR, OCR failed) is transient and never cached. Decision 57: FORM_VARIANTS is the one list of each form's real variants; _JOINER is what may sit between a number and its variant or a keyword's words; the text-layer floor is per page; CACHE_VERSION 3. Decision 60: _seams() lets a keyword typed w2 find W-2; no letters or digits means no keyword. Decision 62: says() is contains_keyword() as content evidence - a form number counts only within TITLE_CHARS; _seams() reads plurals, keeps numbers out of amounts, takes any apostrophe. Decision 63: dominant_forms() - a form number counts in the text when it is in the title or is the number the document mentions most; form <anything> is a form number. Decision 64: dominant_forms() weighs a mention by its shape - a form names itself with its year or revision and another form in a sentence. Decision 66: the title is weighed the same way (_title_forms(); _REFERENCE_BEFORE marks a form quoted after attach/forms/see/of/on/and/or), a number outside FORM_VARIANTS is a mention only after Form, a keyword's words sit on one line or wrap as a heading from a line's start (_WRAPPING_JOINER, _LINE_START), a sheet's cells are tab-separated within a row; CACHE_VERSION 5. Decision 67: what comes before a form is read before what follows it (attach Form 1098 (2025) is a reference); a title naming _LIST_OF_FORMS or more forms names none; the title window is measured on the lower-cased text; _LINE_START admits a bullet, a pipe or a rule. Decision 68: _LIST_OF_FORMS counts families (_FAMILY), so a consolidated 1099 is one family's document; _REFERENCE_BEFORE stays on one line. Decision 69: a form number set off by a dash is a reference (_REFERENCE_AFTER), a dash before the year is still dated (_SELF_AFTER), and _REFERENCE_BEFORE reads across a line break again. Decision 73: says() weighs where a plain keyword is said, not only that it is there - an occurrence that is a menu line's title (_menu_tails: a form number and the title a dash or a comma sets off from it are one reference) or what an ask-word asked for (_asked_for: attach, provide, send, see and their kin, governing the rest of their own sentence and the line a request wraps on to) is the page talking about a document rather than being one, and one occurrence that is neither is enough. A dash-set-off form that heads its line with a year beside it, where the title window holds no second such line and no ask precedes it, names itself (_titles_its_own_line), so a payer's substitute form is not read as a checklist. A form number after a comma continues a list (_LIST_CONTINUES), and enclosed/enclosure/enclosures/re: join _REFERENCE_BEFORE, which now reads a colon between the word and the form. any_keyword_matched() answers the router's question 'did this row's keywords match, apart from the year?'. CACHE_VERSION 6. Decision 82: a verdict keeps the evidence behind it. Evidence(rule, term, where, page) is the one shape - EVIDENCE_RULES (required, any, date, filename, refused) and EVIDENCE_PLACES (title, first_page, footer, deep) are the named values, imported by the router, the index and the app's vocabulary and retyped nowhere. The Evidence record, those two lists and the cell format that format_evidence() writes and parse_evidence() reads now live in tracker/records.py (decision 100) and are re-exported here for one release; what stays here is the reading of a document that produces them. says() became a thin wrapper over _says_where(), which reaches the same verdict by the same reading and also says where the word was found (_where_said(): the title window first, then a page's last _FOOTER_LINES non-blank lines, then the rest of page 1, then deep), so no placement moved. evaluate_rules() puts an Evidence per matched rule on ContentResult.evidence, on a failing verdict too, and the reason sentence is untouched; the date rule records the row's Period, not the regex it derives and not a word of the document. format_evidence()/parse_evidence() are the one owner of the index cell's compact form (term@where:page rule, candidates joined by '; '), and the page is left off when it is 0. CACHE_VERSION 7, because a version-6 verdict read back would claim a verdict with no reason behind it. Decision 85: a form heading its own line with its printed title after its number and its year after the title names itself, at the weight a bare number-then-year mention carries - _names_itself() is the one predicate, and it holds both shapes a printed title wears (a dash between number and title, decision 69/73's; or nothing between them, _SELF_TITLED). The IRS's 2024 and 2025 W-2 revisions print one copy to the page, so Copy B's only "W-2" is the foot's "W-2 Wage and Tax Statement 2025 Department of the Treasury" and the form said nothing about itself before this. The year must be a year and not a date's tail ("Form 941 04/30/2025" on a CP 575 is a filing deadline), and a page heading two such lines is a menu, as it is for the dashed shape - _lists_forms() counts both. CACHE_VERSION 8, because a cached verdict from before it would say a one-copy W-2 is nobody's form. Decision 90: a keyword may name alternatives and join the phrases one of them wants together, read through manifest.keyword_alternatives() - says() takes the first alternative whose every phrase is said and places the evidence at its leading phrase, contains_keyword() reads a file name the same way, and a keyword holding neither character is one phrase exactly as before. CACHE_VERSION 9, because a verdict cached before it read the '|' and the '+' as words to look for.

The tidy-up at the end of a real pass also removes the retired JSON cache file and any temp file beside it (_remove_the_retired_cache(), by RETIRED_CACHE_FILENAME) - nothing reads it, and the removal is said once on FileReport.attention (RETIRED_CACHE_REMOVED) - on the console, in the app's warnings and counted on the practice page - for that pass only. Originals are moved byte for byte under their own names and never altered. Each drop is handled on its own: a drop that cannot be moved is left in place for the next run, a drop that fails after it was preserved is recorded as Needs Review with the error, and the record is written in a finally block so nothing moved into PBC/ is ever unrecorded. Files the client drops straight into the visible PBC/ are filed and indexed in place; a re-sent document whose working copy vanished from Prepared/ is re-filed rather than called a duplicate; a Document renamed in the editor keeps filing into the folder that already holds its files (assign_folders, not folder_name_for); empty client folders are cleared after sorting. assign_review_file() is the person's counterpart to file_drops(): moves the parked copy under the canonical name (or copies from PBC/ if it is gone), rewrites the index row as Filed with the ASSIGNED_BY_PERSON reason, records the keyword a person typed in the same call, all under the engagement lock. The IndexEntry record and INDEX_LAYOUT live in tracker/records.py (decision 100). HISTORY, kept as history: until decision 102 the index was a workbook rewritten whole on every pass, and decisions 54, 56, 58, 59, 61, 65, 66, 67, 68, 69 and 72 are thirteen readings of what that cost - a snapshot sidecar that outlived its workbook, a deferred write, a stale workbook, a header row a sort had moved, a renamed tab, a column inserted at A; what survives of them here is the reading of bytes (replaced_in_pbc() decides by bytes alone; _copy_whole() leaves no half-written copy; every move is a rename in _move_whole(), because shutil.move copied a held-open drop truncated into PBC; what lies behind a junction is not a drop; a name Windows cannot open is reported every pass; a row recorded without its bytes is tied to them only while its working copy and its original agree, UNTIED_IN_PBC; a recorded original that has left PBC/ is said every pass, MISSING_IN_PBC, and where a stray carries its bytes the row follows the file, MOVED_IN_PBC; REPLACED_IN_PBC and UNTIED_IN_PBC are FileReport.attention, not errors; a parked path a later row records is the later row's; assign reuses an earlier attempt's copy first and leaves an annotated parked copy, saying so). Decision 76: dismiss_review_file() rewrites a parked row NOT_REQUESTED with the DISMISSED_BY_PERSON reason and moves nothing; _find_parked() takes a dismissed row too, so filing it is the undo. Decision 77: unfile_document() is the way back - the working copy returns to 00 - Needs Review under the client's own name, the row is rewritten NEEDS_REVIEW with the UNFILED_BY_PERSON reason, and the engagement is re-scanned (outside the lock, which the scan takes for itself); a working copy that is no longer the row's bytes is left and said out loud (LEFT_FILED). Decision 82: IndexEntry.evidence is the last column, written through records.format_evidence() and read back through records.parse_evidence(); a person's decision leaves it alone. Decision 87: every decision is appended to the record through tracker/ledger.py by one rule, _rows_changed(), read off the rows themselves. DECISION 102 - THE INDEX MOVED INTO THE RECORD: read_index() takes the engagement folder and reads the store's documents table, in the index's own order, after store.follow_the_journal(); _record() is the one write, every event a decision produces in a single store.record() call, and the rollback that puts a moved file back asks _the_record_holds(). The migration that read a legacy folder's index workbook into the journal once, and the request-list import of decision 103 that read the sheet once a pass and journalled its differences, both LEFT WITH DECISION 104 and are set aside outside the tree in Retired - Excel manifest: ensure() is now the store's top-up and the three words that say whether it describes the engagement, it writes nothing in the folder, and every caller drops the flag that used to keep a dry run from migrating. clients_root_of() is store.root_for() under its old name. _storable() keeps only the refusal of a name UTF-8 cannot hold (the journal is UTF-8 JSON); a control character in a POSIX name files again, because the refusal of one existed only because a workbook is XML. A person's filing records its keyword in the SAME store.record() call as the row (_record()'s also), because the filing and what it taught are one decision. THE DELIBERATE CYCLE: _rescan() imports tracker/scanner.py at call time so a person's filing is scanned the moment it lands, and the scanner imports this module's index reader at call time; neither runs at load.
- **`tracker/ledger.py`** — The engagement's own append-only record: one JSON object per line in LEDGER_FILENAME, appended under the engagement lock by every writer, and the ONLY copy of what the machine knows AND of what the person typed - the index, every request's status, the keywords people's filings taught, and (decision 104) the request list and the engagement's details as the app's editor saved them. Owns the event names (preserved, filed, parked, duplicate, assigned_by_person, dismissed_by_person, unfiled_by_person, bytes_recorded, keyword_learned, scanned, rules_changed, drafted, imported, migrated; rules_imported retired - read, never written), their payload keys, append() / read_events() / fold() / statuses() / rules() / apply() / replay() / head(), and the file name.

The fold of these lines - through tracker/store.py, which keeps the fold so that no reader pays for it twice - IS what filer.read_index() returns and what manifest.load_manifest() and manifest.load_engagement_info() answer, and nothing else holds those rows. apply() folds a rules_changed event, and the retired rules_imported an older journal carries, the same way (_apply_rules_event): the rows the event carried replace those identifiers, the ones it names as removed go, the details it carried are set; the create carries the whole list and every save only what moved, so the fold of every event is the list - which is what makes store.rebuild_engagement() able to take everything from the journal alone. RETIRED_EVENTS names what this version reads and never writes: new(), append() and store.record() refuse rules_imported by sentence (RETIRED_EVENT), and a digest an old line carries is simply not read. fold() returns rows in the index's own order, and a row that changed identity keeps the place the one it left held. What keeps it honest is the autouse fixture in tests/conftest.py: after every test a store is built from nothing and held to replay() over these lines - the documents, the statuses and the rules alike. Sits at the bottom beside tracker/locking.py and imports only it: the events are plain dicts, so each writer serialises its own rows with the function in tracker/records.py that owns that shape, and no cycle is created. One os.write of the whole line under O_APPEND then fsync, so a kill mid-append leaves at most a torn tail: read_events() ignores it and the next append() truncates it, and nothing else ever rewrites the file. O_APPEND is atomic for concurrent writers on POSIX and is not on Windows, which is why append() refuses unless locking.lock_is_held() says this process holds the engagement lock. Not SQLite: a database file a cloud client syncs is a corrupted database file. migrated is the one event that carries no row - it named the files decision 102's migration moved aside; nothing writes one since 104, and it stays readable. Rows are keyed by the original's PBC location; a row that followed an original the client moved carries the identity it left (was), so the fold drops the vacated one. fold() passes over an event name it does not know and read_events() refuses a bad line anywhere but the tail. The reminder writes files and takes no lock, so drafted is reserved; runner and api reach the writers through the filer, the scanner and the manifest and make no call of their own. Decision 115 unreserved DRAFTED: written by the pass under the lock it holds and by the reminder's CLI under one it takes, carrying ASKED_KEY (identifiers asked, in order; [] on a quiet week) or HELD_KEY (identifiers that held the draft), and FILE_KEY / FINGERPRINT_KEY when a file was written - identifiers only, never a word of the email; appended only when something moved. day_of() is the one reading of a stamp, the local day it fell on, beside stamp() the one writing.

EngagementLock (the open handle and its token), EngagementLockedError; engagement_lock() context manager, taken before the request list, the record or the drop folder is read.

The descriptor stays open while held (Windows then refuses to delete it, so a stale-looking lock its owner still holds is refused) and release_lock() removes the file only if it still carries this run's token. RUN_TIME_LIMIT_SECONDS is the one number for how long a scheduled pass may run: tracker.scheduling renders it as the task's ExecutionTimeLimit and STALE_LOCK_SECONDS is derived above it. One machine per clients root: a lock file synced between two machines is not a lock. lock_status()/clear_stale_lock() back the app's lock notice. Decision 54: pid_alive() - a lock whose owner process is gone is stale at any age. Decision 56: the lock line carries host=; another host's pid is unknowable, never dead. Decision 59: a lock that cannot be deleted on release is marked RELEASED_LINE. Decision 102: the lock is not re-entrant - it is an O_EXCL file - so the steps a pass makes take a lock_held flag and skip taking it, and a writer that may be reached with the lock already held (manifest.save_rules(), the journal's append) asks lock_is_held() rather than taking it twice. A document matching one row's required keywords but failing its other rules is contested and blocks its own filing — misfiling a tax document is worse than not filing it. When nothing routes, the reason is the most useful one available: a document whose content fits a row that refused the file (size floor, type, unreadable PDF) is reported as CONTESTED_PREFIX, and a file every row refused for the same reason carries that reason. A file name is read the same whole-token way a keyword is, run-together spelling and all (W2 for W-2), but only ever as evidence for a person. Eligibility is has_routing_rules(): keywords or a typed year; a year derived from Period only checks a document a keyword already matched. Decision 55, as decision 92 left it: a text layer extract() marked needs_ocr is no text at all, so a multi-page scan is read no further than a one-page one - and where 55 then filed it on its name, it now parks. Decision 58: no run-together fallback; the keyword pattern already reads a dash or space as optional. Decision 73: a row whose any-keywords all matched and whose year alone failed is remembered as a lead, and a file that would otherwise be parked with 'matched no request' is parked as 'looks like J01 (expected period not found ...)' with J01 as its candidate - the sentence a contested file gets, so the reminder asks the client about the period. A lead pre-empts no filing, unlike a required-keyword match, so the decision is exactly as it was; only the reason and the candidates improve. The Routing record and EVIDENCE_CONTENT live in tracker/records.py (decision 100) and are re-exported here for one release: the decision is a record, this module is the deciding. Decision 82: Routing.evidence_record is why, beside Routing.evidence, the tier the decision rested on - EVIDENCE_CONTENT or nothing, since decision 92 removed EVIDENCE_FILENAME (nothing rests on a name; content_check.RULE_FILENAME, the word an index row actually carries, is untouched and still produced). Keyed by candidate identifier: the content check's own Evidence tuple for a row that was read, _filename_evidence() for what the name said (a name is all title and has no page), and _refusal_evidence() for a tier-2 refusal, which travels as reasons.Reason.code rather than the sentence a person reads. _recorded_for() cuts it down to the identifiers the decision names, because every row considered leaves something behind and one index cell must not carry the whole manifest's workings. It decides nothing: every verdict is reached exactly as it was before there was a record. Decision 84: a blocked file - content fits a row, the same row's tier-2 rules refused the file - keeps the verdict's evidence beside the refusal in record, because the refusal alone says which rule said no and never which request the document looked like. The verdict was already read there to decide the file was blocked, so nothing is computed twice and no placement moves. Decision 92, the owner's (2026-09-18): A DOCUMENT NOBODY CAN READ IS FILED BY NOBODY. The by-name tier is gone - when no word of the file could be read (a scan with no text layer OCR could not rescue, an image-only PDF, an empty sheet) no row is a candidate, and the file parks with reasons.NO_READABLE_TEXT (router.UNREADABLE), which is deliberately not UNMATCHED: nothing was matched against anything, and the fix is OCR or a person, never another keyword. _filename_evidence() stays and is recorded on the parked row, so review.triage() offers the request the name points at at RULE_STRENGTH's weakest tier and the app's card and the Status Report show it - a place for a person to start reading, never a filing. _read() no longer skips OCR for a sensibly named scan: nothing is filed on a name, so OCR is the only thing that can still file one, and the scan whose name says W-2 is exactly the one whose content must be read (the _filename_hit shortcut went with the skip). The cost was stated and accepted: until Tesseract is installed every scanned PDF parks - twelve rows of the firm's own corpus moved from filing to parking, and two the name had been misfiling now park instead. Decision 93 (a row per issuer): an issuer row is an ordinary row carrying the entity's name in Required Keywords, and which row wins needed no new rule - a required keyword is the strongest tier and the generic K-1 row has none, so the issuer row takes the K-1 that names it. The one rule added is the park: when any row narrows the row that accepted a document (manifest.narrowing_rows over the rows this pass considers, so an issuer row set aside as Override.NOT_APPLICABLE is nobody's issuer) and none of the narrowing rows matched, nothing is filed - reasons.ISSUER_NOT_NAMED, the narrowing rows named, shortlist led by the row that did accept it. Filing on the generic row would put two entities' K-1s in one folder; taking the row left over would be guessing by elimination. Decision 107: whether a page counts two forms as its own is content_check.own_forms(), the same reading the scanner's miss path makes; computed once in route_file() and handed to evaluate_rules() for the ordinary reading and to the split alike, so a page that prints two forms' own names never files on a third form it merely mentions (decision 94's rule, by construction); the forms are then taken in first-mention order (self_named_forms) for the filing order, and _multi_form() decides exactly as before. Decision 105: the split's verdicts are remembered too. _multi_form() takes route_file()'s keep closure and calls it for every row it files a copy under, with the second reading's verdict, after the ordinary reading has left its own refusal - the verdict the router files on is the one the scan must find, or the second copy fails validation on the next pass and the client is asked for a form they already sent. A page that parks keeps nothing new.

WHERE IT LIVES IS THE POINT: never under the clients root and never in an engagement folder, because those sync and a synced database file is a corrupted one - decision 87's finding, kept, with the owner's 2026-09-19 decision adding the local database the other side of that line. The journal stays in the folder and travels with the engagement; the store is local and disposable, and the arrow only points one way - the store is rebuilt from the journal, never the reverse. THE GUARANTEE is journal-then-apply: record() refuses outside the engagement lock and refuses a retired event name by sentence, appends each event through append() and only then folds them in one BEGIN IMMEDIATE, so a machine that dies between the two leaves the journal ahead and sync() replays the difference. The fold has one owner, apply() in tracker/ledger.py, so a line-at-a-time replay and a whole-file fold cannot differ. ONE CONNECTION PER PROCESS: connect() opens it on first use and every writer deep in the package asks for it by name; close() lets it go, which Windows needs before a database file can be deleted. TRACKER_STORE overrides where it is - the suite points every test at its own file. It imports records, ledger and locking and nothing else of the package at load time - narrower than its layer allows, so the database the readers answer from never depends on the modules that walk folders and move files; connect() reads tracker/settings.py at call time and the CLI imports the registry at call time to find the folders. A version-1 file is refused by the sentence open() has always had, and is deleted and rebuilt: the store is disposable and no store at the office predates this chain. key_root() is the one rule for the key an engagement is stored under (root_for() is its name for a caller with no root in hand): the root the settings file names whenever the folder is under it - the record's own root, which wins over the root a caller typed, so a pass run on one client's folder and a check given the drive key the engagement as the app does - else the caller's root, else the folder's parent. _engagement_row() answers by that exact key, and under the recorded root by nothing else: a folder there with no row is one the store has not met, never another engagement whose key its path ends with (decision 106; the pre-integration audit found Clients/Archive/Smith 2025 answered as Clients/Smith 2025's row). The tail - the one stored path the folder ends with, longest wins - answers only where no recorded root covers the folder, which is decision 103's end-to-end finding on a machine with no settings file. Decision 107: the verdict cache's two tables are per engagement and cascade with it; cached_verdicts() returns the memos and the verdicts at the CACHE_VERSION the caller names as plain dicts and JSON text (this module never learns the verdict's record - test_layers pins that it imports nothing above it); remember_verdicts() deletes the rows at other versions, the paths and digests pruned, and upserts what was learned, refusing outside the lock and for an unknown engagement by the two sentences record() uses (_held_under_the_lock()). A version-2 file is refused by the same sentence a version-1 file was. RULE_COLUMNS is built from records.RULE_FIELDS; _rule_from_sql() hands the list fields back as lists and the flag as a boolean, the shape the API hands the editor. Decision 115: last_event() answers the newest event of a name for an engagement (or the newest carrying a key) from the events table - what the reminder compares this week's draft with, and what the runner reads the last draft day from.

Decision 63: the prior-year return rows require their form number and title, so a return wins over its schedules' lines. Decision 64: the return rows require their title phrase, not their number; the K-1 row keys on the K-1's title; tests/irs/ (the IRS's own forms) and tests/test_irs_forms.py route them all. Decision 65: every prior-year return row requires the jurat; schedule rows key on their titles, not on account names. Decision 66: no row keys on a line every return prints (dividends and distributions, ownership percentage, donation) or the organizer asks (child care provider); the receipt, list and childcare rows key on those documents' own titles. Decision 67: the receipt row does not key on contribution statement (an IRA's, a 529's); the childcare row knows the provider's statement; the estimated tax row keys on a voucher's own lines (its numbered heading, the amount line), not the booklet's prose. Decision 68: the receipt row keys on receipt wording only (a pledge, a thank-you and the firm's letter are not receipts); the estimated tax row knows the state voucher; the childcare row does not take an FSA administrator's statement. Decision 69: the receipt row keys on words only a charity prints; no form 540-es; L01 has no tuition statement (a checklist's line, a university's bill). Decision 72: item_from_spec() reads a spec's lists through manifest.csv_tuple(), the one parser, rather than a copy of it. Decision 73: the shared estimated-tax row is two rows, because an individual's 1040-ES voucher is not a corporation's record (business_estimated_tax keys on corporation estimated tax, estimated tax voucher, estimated payments made); the December bank row does not key on statement of account (a credit-card issuer's and a broker's heading) and takes a workbook, as the reconciliation it asks for arrives; the property tax row keys on the bill's own titles, not on assessor, parcel number or property tax bill (an assessor's notice and a servicer's escrow analysis print those); D01 drops thank you for your donation (every fundraiser's salutation); I01 drops advance payment of premium tax credit (a marketplace notice's sentence); J01 keys on child care/day care spellings with the run-together copies deleted, since the matcher reads the space as optional; 1041 A01 names the kind of trust (an IRA custodian's paperwork is a Trust Agreement too), B02 drops year-end account statement (a bank's heading), C01 drops distribution schedule (a mutual fund's), E01 knows stepped-up basis; 990 C02 keys on the schedule's own title rather than compensation of officers (Part VII's line and the Statement of Functional Expenses', which is now a financial statement's title), D02 on grants made rather than a bare grantee (a letter the charity received) or grants paid (the 990-PF's line 25), E01 without program description (a grant proposal's); the xlsx-only rows and the loans row take the format a client really sends, and officer_comp drops form 1125-e with it (the blank IRS form parks). Decision 85: 1040 E01 knows the wording a broker actually exports - realized gain/loss and the run-together realized gain loss beside the firm's own realized gain and loss - and takes a workbook, since that export arrives as an .xlsx as often as a CSV; 1041 B01 takes the same two, because the trust's realized gain/loss export is its 1099-B by another name. No IRS form in tests/irs/ says either word, and decision 68's consolidated 1099 never prints them, so the composite's placements are untouched. Decision 90, the owner's catalog: _prior_return() writes every prior-year return row's required keyword, with JURAT as the one owner of the line decision 65 added, and a state return's own printed title as an alternative inside that keyword - a standalone CA 540 or NY IT-201 files 1040 B01 on 'resident income tax return', a CA 568 or NY IT-204 files 1065 A01 on 'return of income' or 'partnership return', a CA 100S files 1120S A01 on 'franchise or income tax return', and another state is one more phrase, not a rule. The alternative lives inside the required keyword rather than in Any Keywords so the row's required set stays required: the prior-year return still outranks a row that matched on any keyword and one that fails another rule is still contested. The 1040 catalog gains A03-A06, one row per 1099 a person receives, keyed on the form's number - 'nonemployee compensation' is said by the IRS Attention page ahead of every information return and 'certain government payments' by the 1040-ES package, so neither is a keyword; 'miscellaneous information' and 'payment card' are, the second because the 1099-K's title never lands on one line and 'payment card' begins it, where a checklist's menu rule can see it. 'depreciation' joins SHARED - the 1120's C02 unchanged, 1120S F02 and 1065 D02 new - so the schedule behind Form 4562 has one set of words; a fixed-asset register that never says depreciation stays on fixed_assets, which all three catalogs already carry. Decision 93: the catalog keeps ONE K-1 row (1040 F01, K1_CATALOG/K1_IDENTIFIER) and it asks for the state K-1 too - California heads Schedule K-1 (568) "Member's Share of Income" - because which partnerships a client is in is a fact about that client, not about the 1040. issuer_row() cuts a row per issuing entity from k1_row(): same Any Keywords, same period and extensions, the normalised entity name in Required Keywords and in the Document. The 1065's F01 is Special Allocation Support and decision 85's F1 stays open there.
